name: Whitlock
basis: Original setting written for Prospero Dungeon, modeled on real territorial towns of the 1880s.
summary: A copper and silver town of about four thousand people in southeastern Arizona Territory, 1882: a railroad depot and freight yards on the flat, the Sarah Ann mine and stamp mill on the hill, a Main Street of brick and adobe, a Chinese quarter, a Mexican plaza, and ranches and a cavalry post out in the valley.

curated-2026-10.title: Whitlock, Arizona Territory, written for Prospero Dungeon
curated-2026-10.note: An invented town. Its institutions, trades, prices and yearly calendar follow what was usual in territorial mining and railroad towns of the early 1880s (Tombstone, Bisbee, Globe, Silver City, Prescott), drawn from general historical knowledge. Every business and person named is fictional. Rents are weekly, in 1882 dollars. Coordinates are anchored in the Sulphur Springs Valley of southeastern Arizona for distance estimates only; the climate follows that area at about 4,600 feet.

neighborhoods.name: Main Street
neighborhoods.summary: Four blocks of brick and adobe storefronts with wooden awnings: the mercantile, the bank, the assay office, the newspaper, the barber and bathhouse, hotels and saloons.

neighborhoods.name: The Depot and Front Street
neighborhoods.summary: The railroad depot, freight sheds, water tank and stock pens, with Front Street's cheap saloons, chophouses and lodging houses facing the tracks.

neighborhoods.name: Mill Hill
neighborhoods.summary: The Sarah Ann stamp mill, hoisting works and company offices on the slope above town; the stamps pound day and night and you stop hearing them after a week.

neighborhoods.name: Sarah Ann Gulch
neighborhoods.summary: Miners' cabins, tents and company boarding houses strung up the gulch to the shafts, with a company store and two saloons of its own.

neighborhoods.name: Fourth Street
neighborhoods.summary: Plain frame houses and boarding houses east of Main where clerks, mill foremen, teachers and railroad men with families live; washing lines and chicken yards out back.

neighborhoods.name: Courthouse Hill
neighborhoods.summary: The county courthouse, the Methodist church, the schoolhouse and the brick houses of the bank cashier, the mine superintendent and the better-off merchants.

neighborhoods.name: China Alley
neighborhoods.summary: A narrow lane behind Main Street of adobe laundries, a herb shop, a Chinese grocery, a joss house and the vegetable gardeners who sell door to door.

neighborhoods.name: La Plaza
neighborhoods.summary: The Mexican barrio around a dirt plaza with a bandstand, the Catholic church of San Ysidro, flat-roofed adobe houses, a cantina, a panaderia and evening paseos.

neighborhoods.name: Ash Creek
neighborhoods.summary: The creek bottom below town where cottonwoods and willows shade picnic spots, Mexican farmers grow chiles and corn, and boys swim in the deep hole in summer.

neighborhoods.name: Fairground Flat
neighborhoods.summary: Open ground south of the tracks with the racetrack, the county fair sheds, the baseball diamond and the brickyard.

neighborhoods.name: Fort Merritt
neighborhoods.summary: A cavalry post of adobe barracks around a parade ground, six kilometres south on the valley road, with a sutler's store and officers' row.

neighborhoods.name: Turkey Creek ranches
neighborhoods.summary: Cattle ranches spread across the grassland west of town: adobe headquarters, windmills, corrals and line camps.

neighborhoods.name: Kuhn's Hot Springs
neighborhoods.summary: Warm springs in a canyon northwest of town with a bathhouse, a small hotel and shade trees; a Sunday buggy ride out.

neighborhoods.name: Copper Basin
neighborhoods.summary: A smaller mining camp eight kilometres up the range, reached by the daily stage: one street, a hoist, a store, a saloon and a post office.

transit.name: On foot
transit.summary: Most people walk everywhere in town; Main Street to the depot is ten minutes, to the mill a stiff twenty uphill.

transit.name: Horses from the livery
transit.summary: A saddle horse hired from the Union Livery or Ochoa's corral for about two dollars a day, or your own kept at livery.

transit.name: Buggies and wagons
transit.summary: Hired buggies for Sunday drives and doctor's calls, ore and freight wagons on the mill road, spring wagons to the ranches.

transit.name: Whitlock & Copper Basin Stage
transit.summary: A daily Concord coach from the depot to Copper Basin and the hot springs, carrying mail, payroll and passengers.

transit.name: Gila Valley & Northern Railroad
transit.summary: Two passenger trains a day each way to the main line junction, for trips to Tucson, El Paso and the East.

places.name: The Palace Saloon
places.summary: The best saloon on Main Street, with a mahogany bar shipped from St. Louis, a pianist most nights and card tables in the back.

places.name: Brennan's
places.summary: A plain Irish saloon where miners drink beer at five cents a glass and argue about the union and the Fenians.

places.name: Cosmopolitan Hotel dining room
places.summary: White tablecloths, oysters brought in on ice by rail, and a fifty-cent Sunday dinner that the whole town dresses up for.

places.name: Can Can Chophouse
places.summary: A long counter and six tables serving steaks, chops, fried potatoes and pie at all hours.

places.name: Andersson's Bakery
places.summary: Bread, doughnuts and coffee from four in the morning; Mrs. Andersson's cardamom buns sell out by eight.

places.name: City Ice Cream Parlor
places.summary: A cool room with marble tables and ice cream made with ice shipped in by rail; couples come after church.

places.name: Feldman Bros. Mercantile
places.summary: The big general store: dry goods, canned oysters, boots, blasting powder, calico and the latest catalogues from Chicago.

places.name: Mrs. Pruitt's Millinery and Dressmaking
places.summary: A narrow shop of hats, ribbons and dress goods, where fittings take an hour and the news of the town comes free.

places.name: Pioneer Barber Shop and Baths
places.summary: Three barber chairs out front and six tin tubs in back; a hot bath with a clean towel is twenty-five cents, more on Saturday nights.

places.name: Miners' Union Reading Room
places.summary: Upstairs over the bank: newspapers from San Francisco and New York, a few hundred books, chess boards and a stove, open to members and their families.

places.name: Harlan Opera House
places.summary: A two-story adobe hall that hosts traveling theater companies, minstrel shows, lectures, union meetings, church socials and the Saturday dances.

places.name: Wickes' Photograph Gallery
places.summary: A skylit studio where people sit very still for cabinet cards to mail home; a dollar and a half for half a dozen.

places.name: Whitlock Gazette office
places.summary: The newspaper office with its press in the window; people gather outside when the telegraph news is posted on the board.

places.name: Main Street boardwalk
places.summary: The plank sidewalk under the awnings where everyone passes on Saturday evenings to see and be seen.

places.name: Gila Valley depot
places.summary: The red frame depot and platform where half the town turns out to meet the afternoon train and collect mail and newspapers.

places.name: Railroad Eating House
places.summary: Fast plain meals for train passengers and section crews: beefsteak, beans, biscuits and strong coffee for thirty-five cents.

places.name: The Railroad Exchange
places.summary: A Front Street saloon of teamsters, brakemen and freighters, with a faro table and a lunch counter of pickled eggs.

places.name: Freight yards and corrals
places.summary: Sheds, platforms and corrals where ore sacks go out and machinery, flour and barrels come in, worked by teamsters and Chinese laborers.

places.name: Union Livery and Feed
places.summary: A big barn of rental horses, buggies and hay, with a farrier and a boy who will hold your horse for a nickel.

places.name: Kelly's blacksmith shop
places.summary: An open-fronted forge that shoes horses, sharpens drill steel for the mines and mends wagon tyres.

places.name: Stamp mill overlook
places.summary: A spot on the mill road where you can watch ore wagons unload into the forty-stamp mill and see the whole valley to the fort.

places.name: Sarah Ann Company Store
places.summary: The company store for flour, coffee, bacon, candles and work clothes, paid in cash or against next month's wages.

places.name: The Shaft House
places.summary: A tent saloon turned board shack at the head of the gulch, where shifts drink as they come off.

places.name: Mrs. Trevithick's boarding table
places.summary: A long table of Cornish miners eating pasties, stew and saffron cake at twenty-five cents a meal.

places.name: Sam Lee Laundry
places.summary: An adobe laundry of copper boilers and flatirons where shirts are washed, starched and ironed for ten cents.

places.name: Quong Kee herb shop
places.summary: Drawers of dried roots, teas and remedies; Dr. Quong takes pulses and prescribes for miners who distrust the company doctor.

places.name: Wing Hop Kitchen
places.summary: A small kitchen serving noodles, rice and roast pork, and American breakfasts for railroad men at dawn.

places.name: China Alley joss house
places.summary: A small temple with incense, red paper and a carved altar, busiest at New Year.

places.name: La Plaza and bandstand
places.summary: The dirt plaza under pepper trees where families walk in the evening and a band plays on Sundays and fiesta nights.

places.name: San Ysidro Church
places.summary: A whitewashed adobe church with a bell brought from Sonora; Mass on Sundays and weddings on Saturdays.

places.name: Cantina La Sonorense
places.summary: A cool adobe cantina with mescal, beer and a guitar player, and tamales on Saturday nights.

places.name: Panadería Ochoa
places.summary: An outdoor beehive oven turning out pan dulce, bolillos and coffee with canela.

places.name: Fonda Carrillo
places.summary: A family dining room off the plaza serving carne seca, frijoles, tortillas de harina and menudo on Sunday mornings.

places.name: First Methodist Church
places.summary: A frame church with a bell tower, Sunday services, a Wednesday prayer meeting and ice-cream socials.

places.name: Courthouse square
places.summary: The only lawn in town, watered by hand, with young ash trees and benches where the band plays on the Fourth.

places.name: Mrs. Hale's boarding house table
places.summary: A respectable boarding house where teachers and clerks take meals at seven dollars a week; Sunday chicken is the event of the week.

places.name: Ash Creek picnic grounds
places.summary: Cottonwood shade by the creek where families picnic on Sundays, couples walk, and the deep hole is good for a swim in summer.

places.name: Ash Creek trail
places.summary: A path along the creek past farm plots and willow thickets to a small waterfall after the summer rains.

places.name: Whitlock Driving Park
places.summary: A half-mile dirt track with a wooden grandstand for horse races on holidays and trotting matches most Sundays.

places.name: Fairground baseball grounds
places.summary: A rough diamond where the Whitlock Nine play the fort and the Copper Basin club on Sunday afternoons.

places.name: Kuhn's Hot Springs bathhouse
places.summary: Plank bathhouses over warm mineral pools, recommended for rheumatism and miners' aches; fifty cents a soak.

places.name: Kuhn's Springs Hotel
places.summary: A small adobe hotel with a shaded porch and a set chicken dinner for day visitors.

places.name: Fort Merritt sutler's store
places.summary: The post trader's store and bar where soldiers buy tobacco, canned peaches and beer, and civilians hear the fort news.

places.name: Fort Merritt parade ground
places.summary: The square where the cavalry drills and the band plays at retreat; townspeople ride out for Sunday guard mount.

places.name: Copper Basin stage stop
places.summary: A log store and saloon where the stage changes horses and passengers get coffee and a plate of beans.

places.name: Sarah Ann mess house
places.summary: The company mess house by the mill where shift men eat beef, beans, pie and coffee at plank tables for thirty cents.

places.name: Mill Road Saloon
places.summary: A board saloon halfway down the mill road where millmen stop on the way home, with a stove and a checkerboard.

places.name: Sarah Ann pay window
places.summary: The barred window in the company office where the line forms on the tenth of the month and wives wait to meet their men.

places.name: Mill machine shop
places.summary: The company machine shop and foundry where stamp shoes are cast and broken pump parts are made new.

places.name: Sarah Ann change house
places.summary: A steamy shed at the shaft head with hot water, benches and hooks, where miners wash and change out of wet clothes.

places.name: Gulch Methodist chapel
places.summary: A plain board chapel the Cornish miners built themselves, known for loud hymn singing and a carol service at Christmas.

places.name: Hagen's corner grocery
places.summary: A corner grocery with a cracker barrel, kerosene, eggs from the back yard and a running account for every family on the street.

places.name: First Baptist Church
places.summary: A new frame church with a Sunday school, a strawberry festival in May and baptisms in Ash Creek.

places.name: Whitlock Hose Company No. 1
places.summary: The volunteer fire company's hall and hose cart shed, with a dance on the first Saturday of the month.

places.name: Mrs. Osgood's lunch room
places.summary: A front-parlour lunch room serving soup, cold meat and pie to clerks and railroad men who live nearby.

places.name: County courthouse
places.summary: The brick courthouse with a cupola, where people take a seat in the gallery to follow a good trial.

places.name: Ladies' Library Association rooms
places.summary: Two rooms behind the courthouse with donated books, magazines from the East and a dollar a year subscription.

places.name: Whitcomb's lunch counter
places.summary: A counter across from the courthouse where lawyers, jurors and witnesses eat stew and pie between sessions.

places.name: Kwong Wo general store
places.summary: A Chinese general store of rice sacks, dried fish, tea, firecrackers and letters held for men who have no address.

places.name: Herrería Ruiz
places.summary: A smithy off the plaza that makes window grilles, spurs and cooking irons, and mends anything brought to the door.

places.name: Gallegos farm stand
places.summary: A brush ramada by the road where the Gallegos family sells green chiles, squash, melons and corn from their creek plots.

places.name: Molino Baca
places.summary: A small water-powered grist mill on the acequia where farmers bring wheat and corn to be ground for a share of the flour.

places.name: Tafoya's kitchen
places.summary: A farmhouse kitchen that sells tamales, posole and coffee to picnickers and teamsters on the creek road.

places.name: Whitlock brickyard
places.summary: Clay pits, drying racks and a kiln turning out the red brick for every new store front on Main Street.

places.name: Schuster's beer garden
places.summary: A German brewer's garden of lager, pretzels and sausages under a brush arbour, with a brass band on Sunday afternoons.

places.name: County fair sheds
places.summary: Long open sheds for stock and produce shows, used the rest of the year for roller skating and the Fourth of July dinner.

places.name: Suds Row
places.summary: The adobe huts of the company laundresses at the edge of the post, with tubs steaming outside and children underfoot.

places.name: Fort Merritt post library
places.summary: A reading room in the adjutant's building with newspapers from home, a few hundred books and a school for soldiers' children.

places.name: The Halfway House
places.summary: A roadhouse on the valley road just off the military reservation, where troopers spend their pay on whiskey and stew.

places.name: Diamond K ranch headquarters
places.summary: An adobe ranch house with corrals, a blacksmith shed and a windmill, where neighbors help at branding time.

places.name: Turkey Creek store and post office
places.summary: A one-room store with flour, coffee, cartridges and the ranch mail, and a bench out front for talking cattle prices.

places.name: Turkey Creek schoolhouse
places.summary: A one-room adobe school that clears its desks for dances, spelling bees and Sunday preaching.

places.name: Roundup chuck wagon
places.summary: The cook's wagon at the spring and fall roundups, feeding cowhands sourdough biscuits, beef and beans at dawn.

places.name: Turkey Creek stock tank
places.summary: A windmill and earth tank with a cottonwood beside it, where ranch children swim and riders water their horses.

places.name: Kuhn's picnic grove
places.summary: Sycamores and tables below the bathhouse, where Sunday parties spread their baskets after a soak.

places.name: Kuhn's canyon trail
places.summary: A footpath up the canyon from the springs to a seep with ferns and a view back over the valley.

places.name: Kuhn's dairy
places.summary: The Kuhn family's milk cows and spring house, selling butter, buttermilk and cheese to visitors and to the hotel.

places.name: Copper Basin store
places.summary: The camp's only store, selling powder, candles, canned goods and whiskey by the bottle, and the only true scales in camp.

places.name: Widow Ames's boarding table
places.summary: A tent kitchen with a long table where miners eat stew, biscuits and dried-apple pie twice a day.

places.name: Copper Basin post office
places.summary: A shelf of pigeonholes in a log cabin, where the whole camp gathers when the stage brings the mail.

places.name: Copper Basin smithy
places.summary: A lean-to forge where drill steel is sharpened by the hundred and the stage horses are shod.

colleges.name: Professor Lindqvist's assay and mineralogy classes

careers.name: Hard-rock miner
careers.summary: Ten-hour shifts underground in the Sarah Ann for four dollars a day, drilling, blasting and mucking by candlelight.

careers.name: Stamp mill hand
careers.summary: Feeding ore and tending the amalgam plates at the stamp mill on day or night shift, in constant noise.

careers.name: Assayer
careers.summary: Testing ore samples with furnace and balance for the company and for prospectors who bring rocks in a sack.

careers.name: Telegraph operator
careers.summary: Keying train orders and messages at the depot, the first in town to hear any news.

careers.name: Railroad brakeman
careers.summary: Riding freights to the junction and back, setting brakes on car roofs and coupling cars in the yard.

careers.name: Freighter
careers.summary: Driving ore and freight wagons behind twelve-mule teams between the mill, the depot and the camps.

careers.name: Stagecoach driver
careers.summary: Driving the daily Concord to Copper Basin and the springs with the mail and sometimes the payroll.

careers.name: Ranch hand
careers.summary: Riding for the Turkey Creek outfits for thirty dollars a month and found: fences, windmills, roundup and branding.

careers.name: Blacksmith
careers.summary: Shoeing horses and mules, sharpening drill steel and mending wagons at the forge.

careers.name: Store clerk
careers.summary: Measuring calico, weighing coffee and keeping the ledger behind the mercantile counter, six days a week.

careers.name: Bank clerk
careers.summary: Counting gold coin and keeping accounts at the bank, in a starched collar and sleeve garters.

careers.name: Printer's devil and typesetter
careers.summary: Setting type by hand and inking the press for the weekly Gazette, working late before press day.

careers.name: Hotel clerk
careers.summary: Keeping the register and the keys at the Cosmopolitan and meeting every train.

careers.name: Cook
careers.summary: Cooking for a hotel, chophouse or boarding house from before dawn, on a wood range.

careers.name: Laundress
careers.summary: Washing, boiling, starching and ironing other people's shirts and linens by the piece.

careers.name: Dressmaker
careers.summary: Making and altering dresses from catalogue patterns for fittings in the shop or at customers' homes.

careers.name: Schoolteacher
careers.summary: Teaching forty children of every age in one room for sixty dollars a month, and boarding with a local family.

careers.name: Doctor
careers.summary: Company and town doctor: mine injuries, fevers, confinements and buggy calls to the ranches at night.

careers.name: Deputy sheriff
careers.summary: Serving papers, collecting taxes and keeping order for the county sheriff, mostly on foot along Main Street.

careers.name: Saloon pianist
careers.summary: Playing popular songs and waltzes at the Palace from supper until the small hours, and for dances on Saturdays.

careers.name: Bartender
careers.summary: Pouring whiskey and beer and keeping the peace behind a saloon bar.

careers.name: Cavalry trooper
careers.summary: Thirteen dollars a month at Fort Merritt: stables, drill, escort duty and long scouts in the mountains.

employers.name: Sarah Ann Consolidated Mining Company
employers.summary: Owners of the Sarah Ann mine, hoisting works and company store; the biggest payroll in town.

employers.name: Sarah Ann forty-stamp mill
employers.summary: The stamp mill that crushes the company's ore and custom ore from smaller claims.

employers.name: Gila Valley & Northern Railroad
employers.summary: The branch railroad: depot, telegraph, section gangs and freight crews.

employers.name: Feldman Bros. Mercantile
employers.summary: The biggest store in town, which also runs freight wagons to the camps.

employers.name: Sulphur Valley Bank
employers.summary: A brick bank with a Hall's safe that holds the mine payroll and the ranchers' accounts.

employers.name: Whitlock Gazette
employers.summary: The weekly Republican paper, with a job-printing business on the side.

employers.name: Cosmopolitan Hotel
employers.summary: The best hotel in town: forty rooms, a dining room and a bar.

employers.name: The Palace Saloon
employers.summary: Main Street's best saloon, open day and night.

employers.name: Whitlock & Copper Basin Stage Company
employers.summary: Runs the daily coach, the mail contract and a freight wagon line.

employers.name: County Sheriff's Office
employers.summary: The sheriff, three deputies and the jail in the courthouse basement.

employers.name: Fort Merritt
employers.summary: Two troops of cavalry, with civilian blacksmiths, cooks and laundresses on the post.

employers.name: Turkey Creek Cattle Company
employers.summary: The largest ranch in the valley, running several thousand head.

employers.name: Rancho Ochoa
employers.summary: An old Sonoran family ranch with cattle, horses and a corral in town.

employers.name: Whitlock School District
employers.summary: The public school and its elected board.

employers.name: Sam Lee Laundry
employers.summary: The busiest laundry in China Alley.

employers.name: Mrs. Pruitt's Millinery and Dressmaking
employers.summary: Hats, dress goods and dressmaking for the town's women.

career_hubs.name: The mine and mill
career_hubs.summary: Shafts, hoists, the stamp mill and the assay office; the work that keeps the town alive.

career_hubs.name: The depot and freight yards
career_hubs.summary: Trains, wagons, livery barns and smithies by the tracks.

career_hubs.name: Main Street trade
career_hubs.summary: Stores, the bank, hotels, saloons, laundries and shops.

career_hubs.name: The valley
career_hubs.summary: Ranches and the cavalry post out on the grassland.

climate.summary: High desert at about 4,600 feet: mild sunny winters with frosty nights, a hot dry May and June, and afternoon thunderstorms from July into September that turn the washes to torrents.

months.note: Clear and cold at night; occasional snow on the range.
Cool, with a few winter rains.
Windy; dust blows down Main Street.
Dry and pleasant; wildflowers after a wet winter.
The hottest, driest month; everyone waits for the rains.
Monsoon storms most afternoons, with lightning and flash floods.
Afternoon thunderstorms; the grass turns green.
Clear, mild and dry; the best month.
Cold nights, sunny days, an occasional storm.

annual_events.name: Chinese New Year
annual_events.summary: Firecrackers, red paper and open house in China Alley, with oranges and sweets handed to visitors from town.

annual_events.name: Cinco de Mayo
annual_events.summary: A fiesta on the plaza with a band, speeches, dancing and food stalls.

annual_events.name: Fourth of July
annual_events.summary: Parade, oration at the courthouse, hand-drilling contests between mine crews, horse races at the Driving Park and a dance at night.

annual_events.name: Payday Saturday
annual_events.summary: The Saturday after the mine pays out each month, when Main Street fills, the stores stay open late and the saloons are full.

annual_events.name: Saturday dances
annual_events.summary: Dances at the opera house with a fiddle and piano, quadrilles and waltzes until midnight.

annual_events.name: The rains come
annual_events.summary: The first big thunderstorm of summer, when people stand in the street to smell the wet creosote.

annual_events.name: Mexican Independence Day
annual_events.summary: The grito at midnight on the 15th and a day of music, horse racing and dancing on the 16th.

annual_events.name: County fair and roundup
annual_events.summary: Fall roundup ends with a fair: cattle and produce shows, roping, races and a pie table.

annual_events.name: Fort band concerts
annual_events.summary: The post band plays Sunday afternoon concerts that townspeople drive out to hear.

annual_events.name: Thanksgiving turkey shoot
annual_events.summary: A shooting match for turkeys and a dinner at the Methodist church.

annual_events.name: Christmas ball
annual_events.summary: The grand ball of the year at the opera house, with new dresses, an oyster supper and a midnight march.

annual_events.name: Las Posadas
annual_events.summary: Nine nights of candlelit processions through the barrio before Christmas, ending with tamales and piñatas.

local_color.name: Carne seca
local_color.summary: Beef cut thin, salted and dried on lines in the sun, then shredded and fried with chile, onion and tomato; the Sonoran dish everyone in town learns to like.

local_color.name: Flour tortillas
local_color.summary: Sonoran cooks stretch flour tortillas thin and wide as a platter on the griddle, and miners from every country buy them by the dozen.

local_color.name: Sunday menudo
local_color.summary: A pot of tripe and hominy stew in red chile, served on Sunday mornings and recommended for anyone who spent Saturday night on Main Street.

local_color.name: Christmas tamales
local_color.summary: Families in the barrio spend whole days making tamales of red-chile pork in corn husks for Las Posadas and Christmas Eve.

local_color.name: Pasty
local_color.summary: The Cornish miner's dinner: beef, potato and turnip baked in a thick crust, carried underground in a pail and still warm at noon.

local_color.name: Sourdough biscuits
local_color.summary: Biscuits raised with a crock of sour starter that cooks guard like a savings account; an old prospector is called a "sourdough" for the same reason.

local_color.name: Arbuckles' coffee
local_color.summary: Roasted coffee sold by the pound in Arbuckles' packages with a stick of peppermint candy inside, which camp cooks hand to whoever grinds the beans.

local_color.name: Mescal
local_color.summary: Agave spirit hauled up from Sonora by wagon, cheaper and stronger than the whiskey on Main Street.

local_color.name: A schooner of lager
local_color.summary: Lager beer from the German brewer's cellar, sold cold by the glass or the tall schooner when there is ice from the railroad.

local_color.name: Cousin Jacks
local_color.summary: Cornish miners are "Cousin Jacks" and their wives "Cousin Jennies", from their habit of saying they have a cousin back home who could fill any job going.

local_color.name: High-grade
local_color.summary: Assay talk is everyday talk: rich ore is "high-grade", ore is judged in ounces to the ton, and "high-grading" means a miner carrying rich pieces home in his lunch pail.

local_color.name: "Salted"
local_color.summary: A claim is "salted" when someone has planted rich ore or gold dust in it to fool a buyer, and anything too good to be true is said to be salted.

local_color.name: Tommyknockers
local_color.summary: Cornish miners say the knocking in the rock is the tommyknockers, little mine spirits, and some leave them a crust of pasty to stay on their good side.

local_color.name: Border Spanish
local_color.summary: English in the town is full of borrowed Spanish: "savvy?", "pronto", "vamoose", the "calaboose" for the jail, a "ramada" for a brush shade, and "mañana" for later.

local_color.name: Bucking the tiger
local_color.summary: Playing faro, the favorite saloon card game, whose dealing boxes were often painted with a tiger.

local_color.name: Checking your guns
local_color.summary: A town ordinance says pistols must be left with the hotel clerk, livery or bartender on arriving in town; most people do it, and the deputies remind the rest.

local_color.name: Pay day
local_color.summary: The company pays at the barred window on the tenth of the month, and by evening the saloons, stores and the pawnshop all do a month's business in one night.

local_color.name: The evening paseo
local_color.summary: After the heat breaks, families walk slowly round the plaza in their good clothes, the young people one way and their elders the other.

local_color.name: Watching for the rains
local_color.summary: In July the whole town watches the thunderheads build over the mountains each afternoon; when the rains break the heat, people stand out in it.

local_color.name: The assay office
local_color.summary: The assayer on Main Street crushes, fires and weighs samples for anyone with a sack of rock and a few dollars, and his figures start or end most mining arguments.

prices.per: a shot, a bit or two bits
